item.title: Klara and the Sun, 2026
item.description:
I’ve seen enough: Taika Waititi is no longer riffing on a level that is frickin’ sublime. A quick update for those of you who don’t get your news from DiscussingFilm and/or obsessively listen to “Who? Weekly” in order to keep tabs on Rita Ora: On Saturday afternoon, writer-director Taika Waititi opened Instagram and posted — to his grid! — a less than equanimous reaction to the reviews of his new motion picture “Klara and the Sun,” which was in the process of making less money per screen during its second weekend than the average movie theater employee. It wasn’t the most embarrassing self-own of the pre-midterms weekend (that honor belongs to Michigan congresswoman Hayley Stevens, who committed political suicide on live TV with Anderson Cooper), but I’d argue that Waititi’s faux pas has more to say about how the reality distortion field of today’s media landscape has made it all too easy for highly visible people to misperceive the world around them in a crisis.

“I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years,” the director wrote under an image celebrating the 53-point mismatch between the film’s audience and critics scores on Rotten Tomatoes. “But I do listen to the people, so this Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus became critics. The same people who also hated ‘Jojo Rabbit 😂 🤷🏽‍♂️.’ Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.🗑️😢🫶🏽.”

When I saw that his post had been modified, I assumed that Waititi had deleted the part where he wrote “and another thing: I’m not mad. Please don’t put in the newspaper that I got mad.” In truth, he had simply tweaked the bit where it said that “sad lost souls” like me had settled as critics. Good note! Much as fallen angels plummet from the heavens before landing in the depths of Hell to anguish for all eternity, critics don’t settle for a life of press screenings so much as we pathetically free fall into it, plummeting from the sacred highs of making “Thor: Love & Thunder” to the wretched lows of watching it. It’s that natural eye for editing that explains why “Next Goal Wins” felt like it had been cut with a soccer cleat.


Of course, I don’t take any of this too personally. (Don’t you dare fucking put in the newspaper that I got mad.) For one thing, I was actually quite tolerant of “Thor: Love & Thunder,” if only because I believe that casting Christian Bale as a guy named “Gorr the God Butcher” in and of itself makes that movie better than most of what Marvel was pumping out at the time. For another thing, I haven’t even seen “Klara and the Sun” — not because I was busy when it screened here, or because I live in one of the many countries where its release has been canceled on account of the movie’s supposed awfulness and verifiable lack of public interest, but rather because I adore the Kazuo Ishiguro novel on which it’s based, and I was convinced that hiring the director of “Jojo Rabbit” to adapt such a poignant tale of loss and brokenness would be like hiring Peter Farrelly to remake “The Remains of the Day.” Except worse, because I’ve always felt like the Merchant Ivory version of that book could have used a few gratuitous jokes about Anthony Hopkins’ swollen balls.

The truth is that the perceived quality of Waititi’s film is irrelevant to what I found interesting about his Instagram post, in much the same way as its quality is seemingly irrelevant to everything else as well. And in much the same way as the perceived quality of Waititi’s other films is irrelevant to the hissy fit he decided to throw about this one. Are “the same people who also hated ‘Jojo Rabbit’” in the room with us? Because that Oscar-winning movie is sitting at 81 percent on Rotten Tomatoes (Certified Fresh™!). OK sure, I hated it, but, as we’ve previously established, I am quite literally not “the same people” who hated “Klara and the Sun.”

On the other hand, I would very much consider myself to be among the large cohort of critics who adored Waititi’s earlier features like “Hunt for the Wilderpeople,” “What We Do in the Shadows,” and “Eagle vs. Shark.” I suppose I could look up the aggregator metrics for those movies as well, but there isn’t any need — that most of the people reading this article have even heard of such modest Kiwi treasures is testament enough to the groundswell of critical support they received around the world. Perhaps, if he’d read a review in the last 15 years, Waititi might have been able to put that together for himself.

item.title: Who Killed Alex Odeh?, 2026 - ★★★
item.description:
Times change, the arc of the moral universe bends towards justice, and yet one thing that has remained true for as long as I’ve been alive is that prejudice, bigotry, and explicit displays of racism have always been openly permissible in America — so long as they’ve been targeted at Arabs and/or Muslims. That sad and immutable fact was on full display throughout Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral campaign last year, and the say the quiet part out loud reaction to Abdul El-Sayed’s current senate race has somehow managed to be even worse on both sides of the aisle (Democrats lament that he “doesn’t share our values,” while Republicans straight up just call the guy a jihadist). But anyone old enough to remember 9/11 knows that it didn’t start with the likes of Vicky Paladino, just as I assume that anyone old enough to remember the assassination of Alex Odeh knows that it didn’t start with 9/11.

The sole fatality of a bomb that had been planted at the California office where he served as the West Coast Regional Director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC), Alexander Michel Odeh was murdered on the morning of October 11, 1985, leaving behind his wife Norma and their three young daughters Helena, Samya, and Susan. To this day, his slaughter remains “unsolved.” And yet, as Jason Osder and William Youmans’ scattered but vital documentary “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” makes clear soon after it begins, there’s little doubt as to who was behind the killing.

Indeed, the film establishes that the case was effectively solved within days of the attack, and that all three of the primary suspects — all members of a right-wing terrorist group known as the Jewish Defense League — were only allowed to flee to Israel because powerful forces within the American political system preferred for them to get away with it. And to get away with it. And to get away with it. More than 40 years later, no efforts have been made to prosecute or extradite the presumptive murderers. One of them has even moved back to the United States.

And so, despite affecting the aesthetic and tropes of the true-crime format, “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” directly contradicts the expectations of its supposed genre. Instead of establishing a vast mystery for their movie to explore, Osder and Youmans — one of them Jewish, the other a Palestinian-American — give shape to the galling absence of one. Stunted and searching by design, their film unpacks the sociopolitical context of Odeh’s killing in order to illustrate how the easily Google-able question posed by its title could possibly remain “unanswered” for so long, and even partakes in some light subterfuge as part of an effort to pin down the culprits on camera.

item.title: The Mosquito Bowl, 2026 - ★★
item.description:
There have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II, the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “The Mosquito Bowl” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not.

What differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa.

And for the span of the eight-minute montage during which “The Mosquito Bowl” actually makes good on its title, it’s easy to picture how the famous scrimmage — fought between a roster of impossibly beautiful athletes in their primes — might have been used to backstop a story that accentuated the senseless waste of sending thousands of young men to their deaths. Alas, for the rest of this 126-minute film, that waste is better expressed through Berg’s failure to make anything more of their lives, as the “Spenser Confidential” auteur’s latest Netflix project does almost nothing else to distinguish itself from a genre so well-worn that it’s seemingly run out of ways to blow up a human body.

Why “almost”? I was hoping you wouldn’t ask. For starters, there’s the decision to cast thin-skinned ESPN commentator Pat McAfee as an R. Lee Ermey-inspired drill sergeant. “The Mosquito Bowl” also stands out for how confusingly it conflates the thrill and teamwork of combat sport with the violence and camaraderie of armed conflict; war is presented as both a natural extension of what these boys have been trained to do on the gridiron (to the point that the soldiers briefly diagram their plan of attack as if it were a football play), and also the catastrophe that robbed them of a more innocent purpose. (Berg loves the troops as much as he hates the fact that generals and presidents so wantonly sacrifice their lives.) Someone declares that “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in history,” and yet the film’s characters don’t seem to have any special advantages on the field of battle, as it would be glib to suggest that even the country’s best college running back might be able to slip free of a mortar blast. It’s one thing to argue that football is war, and another, much more asinine thing to argue that war is football.

item.title: A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra, 2026 - ★★★★
item.letterboxd:filmTitle: A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra
item.description:
“Send her the dream.”

This is how it starts. A teenage girl lies supine in a field of grass, a hand on her belly, her breathing filling the soundtrack as if the film itself were her lungs. Then she’s asleep, and a pair of disembodied voices — from within her own mind or perhaps another dimension, whatever that difference might be — begin to discuss what images to screen on the back of her eyelids. Wind chimes. A Colorado Avalanche hat has a wing sticking out on each side for some reason. A bullet casing. They debate that last symbol, but ultimately decide it’s OK. The girl won’t know what it means yet.

How can the voices divine such portents themselves? Perhaps the girl’s life is like a movie they’ve both seen before. Then again, the self-possessed originality that fills every frame of Jacqueline Lentzou’s unforgettable “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra” makes that supposition feel almost impossible. That feeling doesn’t last. By the end of this profound but ethereal wisp of a film, a slender cut of pure cinema that defies convention with the blithe inventiveness of a Björk lyric (or some other brilliant poet writing in their second language), the possibilities seem as boundless as life itself. Maybe even more so.

Needless to say, the “Moon, 66 Questions” writer-director’s remarkable second feature isn’t a typical coming-of-age movie, even if it might sound like one on paper. The usual markers abound, like plenty of angst and music (the songs ranging from Vashti Bunyan and Daniel Johnston to Bryan Ferry and… Vincent Gallo?). Drugs. Dancing. Idle gossip. Self-discovery. Hallway makeouts at school and fights with mom at home. It all smacks of lived experience, and the film’s sketch of a story was inspired by a terrible incident in Lentzou’s native Athens when she was a teenager.

But this is most definitely not a movie about growing up. Cleaving much closer in spirit to the existential unease of Gus van Sant’s “Death Trilogy” than it does to the mottled survivalism that runs through everything from “The Breakfast Club” to “Lady Bird” (though it somehow feels lighter than any of those films), “A Day in the Life of Jo” is less interested in adolescence as a crucible than it is as a transitory state of being — a vulnerable in-between where people are in the process of becoming themselves, winnowing their identities down to one at the same time as they’re pushed towards the sheer infinity of what this world might have in store for them. The indwelling light of Lantzou’s style stretches that time into a microcosm of life itself, reimagining the “ephemeral performance” of being a teenager as the work of a soul on Earth.

item.title: Wildwood, 2026 - ★★★
item.description:
On the one hand, Travis Knight’s “Wildwood” is an epic, eye-popping, and almost unfathomably well-crafted celebration of everything that makes Laika special — of everything that makes the Oregon-based stop-motion studio a singular force for good in a film industry where most companies are less interested in savoring the magic of animation than they are in seeing how many shortcuts they can take without breaking its spell. On the other hand, the remarkable time and care that went into “Wildwood” doesn’t prevent it from being the least enchanting of Laika’s films, even if its flaws help to reinforce the power of a story about how magic can persist in spite of itself.

The longest and most ambitious movie of its kind ever made, this sprawling fantasy saga about the overlap between reality and imagination — about a teenage girl in the Pacific Northwest who ventures into an enchanted kingdom to rescue her toddler little brother after he’s abducted there by a murder of crows — pushes the form to new extremes at a time when the rest of the business is hoping that audiences will learn to settle for less. It’s a mad feat of muchness.

Laika 3D-printed 142,000 different face models, hand-molded 728 individual trees, and used more than 715 miles of brass wire across 1,155 days of production. They created a “Braveheart”-style battle one frame at a time, built a perfect miniature replica of Powell’s City of Books to bring the movie’s version of Portland to life (complete with a Drag Queen Story Hour sign), and even designed tiny little Decemberists posters to adorn the heroine’s living room; she seems to be more of a fan of their post-“The Crane Wife” output, but I’m trying my best not to hold that against her.

That degree of loving attention comes at a massive price, of course (with one negligible exception, each of Laika’s films has cost more and grossed less than the one before it), but studio owner and Nike co-founder Phil Knight can certainly afford it, and it doesn’t hurt that his son is running the shop. Not all Hollywood nepo babies! In lieu of any prolonged fawning over the pursuits of a billionaire heir, let’s just say the Skydance merger would probably seem a bit less cataclysmic if David Ellison were capable of directing something as artful and transcendent as “Kubo and the Two Strings” (or even something as competent and colorful as last summer’s live-action “Masters of the Universe,” for that matter).

Which is all to say that “Wildwood” epitomizes why Laika should be treated like a national treasure: It’s stunning, it’s sincere, it’s possessed by a combination of American moxie and a Ghibli-esque willingness to push young audiences out of their comfort zones, and it’s seemingly at peace with losing enough money to sink any other animation studio on the planet. It is, in so many respects, the ultimate testament to what makes Laika unique. It’s also, in so many others, the first of their movies that doesn’t feel as special as it looks (and sometimes doesn’t look as special as it should feel).

Appropriately enough for a project that suggests Laika’s care may not be enough to preserve its magic, “Wildwood” is a story about losing faith in the wonder of the world. And appropriately enough for a project that still has so much to offer in spite of its flaws, “Wildwood” is also a story about how magic can persist in our lives even after we stop believing in it — even after its child-like purity gives way to something mottled and imperfect.

item.title: Matchbox the Movie, 2026 - ★½
item.description:
Credit where credit’s due: For a film that should never have been made or released in the first place, “Matchbox: The Movie” is somehow arriving at just the right time. Impeccably positioned as a potential harbinger of what’s to come, this bland and frictionless Skydance production — debuting on Apple TV a few short days after “Flyboys” star David Ellison finalized an $111 billion deal to consolidate what’s left of Hollywood under his control — is a perfect crystallization of our new god-king’s taste in cinema.

Like “Ghosted,” “The Family Plan,” and “The Family Plan 2” before it (the latter two of which were also written by David Coggeshall), “Matchbox: The Movie” is an algorithmic chore about workaday Americans who get mixed up in some vaguely comedic spy action, the film’s execution so uninspired that its wish fulfillment premise assumes a tone of patronizing condescension — “what if your shitty little life enjoyed a sudden jolt of excitement?” can be a depressing conceit for a movie that can barely imagine that for itself.

Like “Heart of Stone,” “Fountain of Youth,” and Michael Bay’s “6 Underground” (remember that one?), it plays less like a self-possessed piece of popcorn entertainment than it does a large adult son’s half-remembered idea of how movies used to feel. Like “Terminator: Dark Fate” and “Without Remorse,” it takes the residual appeal of its IP for granted to the point that it fails to supply any appeal of its own. And though “Matchbox: The Movie” is much better than some of these early Skydance classics, its relative quality clarifies the most worrisome thing that’s shared between them: It’s not that all of them are bad, but rather that none of them seem particularly concerned with being good.

item.title: Artificial, 2026 - ★★★
item.description:
In case anyone at the world premiere of Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” wasn’t already thinking of the OpenAI biopic as an unofficial sequel to “The Social Network,” the screening was unexpectedly preceded by a musical performance from Damon Albarn, in which the Blur frontman and occasional movie composer was joined onstage by a youth choir for a rendition of an original dirge he wrote for the film about how we’re all singing our way straight into hell. Sixteen years ago, a bunch of angelic little kids belting out “Creep” was the perfect introduction to a sneering chamber drama about the punks whose self-hatred turned the 21st century against itself. Today, now that Silicon Valley’s nerd Prometheis have graduated from getting revenge on Rooney Mara to threatening the future of the human race, the kids are back for a more existential lament. They haven’t grown up, and neither have we.

Once upon a time, a snively Harvard undergrad rewired the entire world only to discover that he couldn’t escape the empty pit of his own soul. Less than two decades after that, another Peter Thiel-funded sociopath bet our species on transcending the limits of humanity, only to prove that we can’t help but encode it into everything we create. It’s the same old story all over again, albeit presented here at the scale that computer scientist Ilya Sutskever (“Anora” breakout Yura Borisov) spent most of his career desperate for the data to achieve. History repeats itself, first as tragedy, second as farce — or in this case, as an uncanny sort of San Francisco camp.

To be honest, I struggled to imagine why a sensualist like the director of “Challengers” and “Call Me by Your Name” would be interested in something as cold and algorithmic as the story of OpenAI. Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as a machiavellian queen bee with a penchant for upspeak and a frighteningly blasé attitude toward replacing mankind with computers (imagine an apocalyptic gay cross between Regina George and Agent Smith), has suggested that Guadagnino was exploring “how far we can take our obsession with not being human before we return to the body,” but this movie never strays far enough from the body to require a return. Garfield’s bulging arms. Borasov’s patchy hair, already receding into lines of code when the movie first introduces Sutskever at the age of 17. Monica Barbaro’s oaken brown eyes, which lend OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati the patina of a moral code. Even the pancreas of a character’s unseen wife, the sickness in which AIG promises to double back and cure if only everyone keeps hurtling forward. “Artificial” focuses its attention on these details as if it were training a neural network to create associations between them.

To “yes, and” Garfield’s supposition, perhaps it would be more accurate to say that Guadagnino is exploring how difficult it is to abandon the body in the first place — and not just the body, but the intangible essence that it contains. We couldn’t leave it behind if we tried, and this, in his own way, is Guadagnino trying just as hard to do that as Sam Altman ever did.

item.title: Behemoth!, 2026 - ★★★½
item.description:
Purposefully unfolding like a piece of classical music that’s lost its melody among a maze of overlapping leitmotifs, Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” is a much slippier and more elegant thing than the scale implied by its title — the deception of which is purposeful as well. Sure, there are car crashes, crane shots, and nine different composers to the film’s credit (with giants of the form like Alan Silvestri, Michael Giacchino, and James Newton Howard each contributing their own diegetic accompaniments), but all of those outsized flourishes have the strange effect of making the elusive film around them feel easier to slip through your fingers.

At its most basic level, “Behemoth!” is a floaty little character study about a hot but avoidant cellist named Alex Sarian (Pedro Pascal) who returns to Los Angeles after 20 years of running away from it and immediately gets seduced back into his memories when he starts working as a session player on a variety of different film scores. Such is the singular effect of movie music — compositions that are inextricably bound to certain images from the moment they’re brought into the world, like a person to the family they never asked to have. Confronted with that strange alchemy for the first time since he abandoned the pictures for the philharmonic, and largely disinterested in the Hollywood slop he’s been hired to play over, Alex can’t help but map the arrangements onto the unresolved moments from his own life.

Maybe, we think, the music will help make sense of the stray thoughts that kick around his head, or at least turn them into the stuff of a “Stardust Memories”-like funhouse to explore. It’s all too easy to imagine what a conventional filmmaker could do with that same concept. But Gilroy, so eager to zag against expectations that he leveraged a mega-budget “Star Wars” show into an uncompromising political thriller about the brick-by-brick sacrifice required to build a rebellion, soon reveals subtler and more ambivalently cinematic intentions than the premise of his latest feature might suggest. By the time “Behemoth!” arrives at its dolcissimo stunner of an ending, it’s all the more rewarding for that.

item.title: Verity, 2026 - ★★★
item.description:
“It Ends with Us” author Colleen Hoover isn’t typically in the business of making women look bad (male writers have all but cornered that particular market since before the invention of the printing press), which is why it’s so curious that the latest movie adapted from her books seems determined to convince us that its title character — a grieving mother who’s been rendered catatonic by a recent car crash, and now requires full-time care from the stern Ukrainian nurse who tube-feeds her in between diaper changes — is actually a demon bitch from hell. Anne Hathaway would never! … or would she?

Faithfully adapted from Hoover’s 2018 bestseller of the same name, Michael Showalter’s “Verity” is a ludicrous psycho-thriller as cold and tart as the wine cocktail that should come free with every ticket. It’s also a film whose enjoyably contrived pleasures, like those of its source material, hinge upon the fact that people are eager for any excuse to look down on a successful woman. And while men are eternally GOATed in that regard, women are just as capable of falling into that trap — especially when they feel that another woman’s success came at the expense of their own. Human nature! Gotta love it.

Indeed, it’s “local author” Lowen Asleigh (Dakota Johnson) who scoffs at the idea of ghostwriting the next installment in Verity Crawford’s ultra-popular book series. It’s Lowen who rolls her eyes at the kind of airport paperbacks that have since made Hoover into a millionaire several times over, and Lowen who grows addicted to the unfinished autobiography that she finds on a USB stick inside a locked drawer of Verity’s writing desk — a self-excoriating but utterly remorseless memoir in which Verity outs herself as one of the book world’s biggest “monsters” since the days of Cathy Ames.

But… we get it. I mean, of course we feel bad that Verity’s young daughter was killed in a canoe accident, even though Nick Antosca’s script reduces the scale of the tragedy as it’s presented in the novel, but the part of our brains that’s been corrupted by true-crime (in addition to centuries of misogynistic suspicion) can’t help but look sideways at the mom for surviving the same event.

Verity built an empire on trash, fell victim to the plot of a bad melodrama, and then drove headfirst into a tree shortly thereafter, abandoning her dreamboat ultra-DILF of a husband (Josh Hartnett as Jeremy Crawford) to solo parent their son in the cavernous glass Jens Quistgaard mansion that her “violent miracle of a career” bought for the family somewhere in upstate New York.

item.title: Digger, 2026 - ★★½
item.description:
Alejandro González Iñárritu and Tom Cruise were made for each other, if no one else. One is a cinematic daredevil whose films are fueled by the tension between ego and mortality — a mad virtuoso obsessed with staging elaborate stunts that externalize his inner being into the stuff of outsized spectacle, and do so with a kamikaze effortfulness so extreme that even (or especially) their most grandiose work can make it seem like the person behind them is hiding from reality instead of rendering it larger than life. The other is Tom Cruise.

By different means, toward different ends, both men have consistently risked their creative and/or actual lives as they’ve reckoned with the limits of what they can accomplish with a movie camera. Through projects like “Birdman,” “Bardo,” and the “Mission: Impossible” sequels, both men have dedicated the most recent stretch of their careers to blurring the line between the art and the artist. Not as a bid to elide some kind of moral reckoning (easy as it is to see Cruise’s ascension into “The Savior of Movies” as a calculated rebrand), but rather as an effort to explore — or transcend — the relationship between reality and the stories that people choose to tell about themselves.

In that light, I suppose it was only a matter of time before Iñárritu and Cruise finally combined their powers/personas to make the ultimate movie about self-delusion. And so we arrive at “Digger,” a raw and modest little movie that has no ambition beyond poking some fun at the absurdity of its own existence.

Just kidding. LOL. ROTFL, even. The third chapter in a loose trilogy of postmodern films examining the value of creativity at a time when reality has become stranger than fiction, “Digger” is a mega-budget “Dr. Strangelove” riff so detached from human truth that its most believable character is a one-eyed animatronic cat named Maggie — a VistaVision satire so high-concept that it would be more accurate to measure its running time in altitude than minutes.

Like “Birdman” and “Bardo” before it, Iñárritu’s biggest swing (and most endearing folly) self-reflexively hinges upon the various ways that people make sense of living in a world that has abandoned its logic. A slow-burn ghost story that seems to be playing into convention even as it sneakily plants the seeds to turn the genre on its head, Dave Boyle’s clever and involving “Never After Dark” starts with a rather familiar premise: A medium is hired to expunge a dark spirit from a big house in the middle of nowhere. That introductory detail proves to be an important clue as to how this movie will play with time, as Boyle’s spare and patient script gradually begins to conflate the thin line between this world and the next with the line between the present and the past — to blur one of those boundaries is also to blur the other. Now you might be thinking: “Isn’t ‘banish a living person to the other side of the veil’ just medium-speak for committing murder?” And… well, yes. But it’s a testament to the detail of Boyle’s film — which is modestly scaled but immersively self-contained — that “Never After Dark” is able to redefine the rules of this mortal coil on its own terms. That starts with the mechanics of Airi’s practice, which are as familiar in function as they are novel in form, and, typical of the “Man from Reno” filmmaker’s work, blend Eastern and Western tropes into the stuff of a singular genre exercise.

item.title: Resident Evil, 2026 - ★★★½
item.description:
It’s hard to tell — and even harder to care — whether a small but attention-starved contingent of “Resident Evil” loyalists actually made a preemptive stink about Zach Cregger’s radical new take on the video game franchise, or if algorithmic rage cycles have become so predictable and endemic to the discourse that everyone just assumed that they had. Whatever the case, this much is clear: Cregger’s singular, madcap, arcade-style riff on the survival-horror series that started it all is a massive and rapidly mutating middle finger to the Comic-Con-brained idea that video game adaptations should just give “the fans” what they think they want.

Cregger’s movie arrives in the wake of 2021’s “Welcome to Raccoon City,” a miserable cosplay which attempted to course-correct the nü-metal nuttiness of Paul W.S. Anderson’s movies by slavishly retelling the story of the first two “Resident Evil” titles. The “Weapons” director’s DLC-like approach to the zombie saga pivots back in the opposite direction with a giddy smile on its face. You’ll find no characters from those PlayStation classics (ditto their more recent sequels), nor any narrative connection to the series’ mythology beyond a shared location and a brief reference to the evil Umbrella Corporation. Easter eggs come by the dozen, but the movie’s fast, freaky undead more resemble — and behave like — the “Last of Us” infected than the slow-moving groaners from the early games.

And yet, for all its creative liberties, this is the first “Resident Evil” movie that actually — and rather viscerally — evokes what it feels like to play “Resident Evil.”

The white-knuckled helplessness of entering a new room and flinching at the way it’s framed to emphasize all the places a monster could jump out. The addictively queasy tug-of-war between wanting to explore the next section and wanting to just say “nope” and turn the whole thing off. The headache of item management, the thrill of blowing a villager’s head off with your last shotgun round, only to see tentacles sprout out of its neck hole as it grows more powerful. Cregger’s side-quest-sized story about a hapless courier has been genetically engineered in an Umbrella Corp. lab as the perfect vehicle for all these sense memories, to the point that his “Resident Evil” better reflects the essence of its source material than any of the previous movies. That’s despite how it eschews the franchise’s melodramatic tone in favor of postmodern glee, and ditches its deep(ly ridiculous) mythology in favor of… well, pretty much nothing aside from some errant anxieties about bringing a kid into a world that’s evolving out of our control. That’s what you get when you hire the guy who made “Weapons,” I suppose.

A lean, gripping, and relentless goof absent any trace of the cart-before-the-horse ambitions that have crushed the life out of blockbuster cinema in the age of I.P., Cregger’s “Resident Evil” is so cut to the bone that it starts mid-sentence and drops its closing title card at what feels like might be the start of its third act. In other words, some poor schmuck is about to have the worst night of his life, and he’s only gonna need about 85 minutes to do it.

We never learn a single detail about why Eliza Lim decided to devote her life to medicine, but the film’s opening flashback — in which a younger version of Yeoh’s role sits apart from her colleagues and brutally eviscerates a blood orange so that she can sew it up again — suggests that she wouldn’t know what to do with a social life if she had one. After doing everything in her power to save people’s lives for so long, she can’t stomach the thought of just waiting for herself to die.

Lucky for her, she may not have to wait as long as she thinks. She’s only been off the job for a few days before some goons snatch her out of her kitchen one morning and take her to a derelict hospital where their boss is already prepped for surgery in the operating theater. Eliza doesn’t know the patient’s name, let alone what’s wrong with him, but it’s clear that she’ll be killed if she doesn’t start cutting into his belly soon.

item.title: Love of Your Life, 2026 - ★★★½
item.description:
Rachel Morrison’s “Love of Your Life” is one of my favorite things, all too rare in today’s Hollywood: A gorgeously shot romantic drama about impossibly beautiful people that still manages to feel real enough where it matters. It’s the kind of smart, heartfelt, mid-weight entertainment that rewards you for surrendering to its logic and savoring how its light cuts through the darkness for 100 minutes — so naturally, since we live in hell, it’s only playing in theaters for a single week before it shuffles off to its forever home on Prime Video. I suppose we should be grateful that Morrison got to make it at all, as this is nothing if not a film that implores us to cherish what we still have left rather than rage at what’s been taken from us.

It starts in a decidedly unromantic place: the emergency room of a Boston hospital, where joyless and withdrawn nurse Maya (Margaret Qualley) heals people as a way of attending to the unspecified family situation that scarred her as a child. Blasting Sharon Van Etten music on the subway and grinding out 18-hour shifts in her scrubs seems to be getting the job done, but happiness is a lot harder to deny when someone becomes determined to share it with you.

In this case, that “someone” is Charlie (Gabriel Basso, far too charming for someone whose breakthrough role was playing J.D. Vance), a Mensa-smart goofball who smiles like a fool, dresses like a jock, and radiates an inner glow that shines a hole right through the lonerism that Maya has always maintained for her own protection. He was adopted at birth, and his worldview has been premised on accepting the love that he’s lucky enough to receive. Maya, by contrast, has a real “love isn’t worth the pain of losing it” vibe that has led her to stay as single and untethered as possible. At least until now.

item.letterboxd:filmTitle: The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd
item.description:
Toward the beginning of Tim Blake Nelson’s “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,” a downhearted but defiantly humane prison drama that skips around in time as it maps an Oklahoma man’s journey from childhood poverty to his taxpayer-funded murder at the hands of the state, someone comments that people don’t get out of prison without a little help. There’s always a guard on the take, a civilian who manages to lend an assist from the outside, or — as the case may be — a creative writing teacher who develops a crush on one of her inmate students. That much is self-evident.

Of ultimately greater interest to Nelson is the fact that people don’t get into prison without a little help either. Despite the infinite vastness of America’s carceral system, precious few of its convicted residents were born with some innate desire to kill. That’s not to say they’re innocent, of course (although far too many of them are), but simply to acknowledge the invisible weight of their circumstances. Nobody prefers a bruised apple, but we readily accept gravity’s role in making it fall from the tree. People do terrible things because they feel they have no other choice — to execute them for that is to ensure they never will. Man is an unknowable creature, and few things unsettle it more than forcing it to live within its mystery.

“The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” endeavors to deny us any other choice, as its nonlinear timeline nakedly manipulates our feelings about its title character. The more sympathetic he becomes, the more we learn about why he’s been sentenced to lethal injection; the more we learn about the monstrousness of his actions, the more aggressively Nelson’s screenplay — inspired by unspecified true events — insists upon his fundamental humanity.

Needless to say, the writer-director does himself a great favor by casting an actor as likable as Scoot McNairy in the part. We first meet Wilson on the day that sets the endgame of his destiny in motion — the day that a beautiful but painfully unloved high school teacher named Karen (a southern-fried Amanda Seyfried) starts her new part-time job teaching fiction to a group of privileged inmates at Oklahoma’s biggest maximum-security prison.

Freshly uncoupled from her abusive husband and desperate for the money she needs to pay for her senile dad’s elder care, Karen doesn’t report to the jail any more willingly than her students once did. Most of the inmates react to her presence like chum in the water (there’s only so much a makeup department can do to soften the spectacle of dropping Amanda Seyfried into a room full of horny criminals who probably haven’t seen another woman in months). Wilson, meanwhile, seizes on the opening to play teacher’s pet. A rangy squirrel of a man whose artistic spirit has been as welcome and noticeable throughout his life as a floater in his eye, Wilson is obviously sincere about taking the class seriously. Still, it’s hard to know if that’s because writing sets him free, or because he enjoys having a pretty woman to look at, or because Karen sets his soul on fire in a way that nothing in this world ever has before. It could be all of the above, or it could be none of them — we may never know for sure, and Wilson probably wouldn’t be able to tell us.

item.title: Misty Green, 2026 - ★★½
item.description:
A raw and biting — or at least vigorously gumming — showbiz character study about a faded Black actress whose entire adult life has been shaped by the peaks and valleys of living in a place that often seems flat on the surface, Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” is preoccupied with the relationship between feast and famine from the moment it starts, and by the Los Angeles-specific tendency for those two conditions to remain worlds apart even when they overlap.

Even when they walk right past each other on Hollywood Blvd., or audition for the same role on a studio lot. Fortune is a fickle thing: One day you’re winning some award on TV, and the next day, a short 18 years later, you’re being evicted from your dead sugar daddy’s beachside pied-à-tierre because he left it to his wife in his will. That’s la la land for ya.

As Rock takes pains to remind us in the photo montage that opens his latest and most serrated film (a film that shares its setting’s lack of subtlety), L.A. is a city where world-class museums are just down the block from Skid Row, where the Oscars are hosted inside of a hideous shopping mall, and where the paparazzi thoughtlessly climb over homeless people to snap photos of starlets like Lindsay Lohan (to name the first of several celebrities this movie catches with a random stray). How is anyone supposed to stop chasing the bag when it feels like, even at their lowest ebb, they’re still always close enough to reach out and grab it? By the same token, how is anyone supposed to have the bag when there’s almost no degree of success that can ensure they’ll let you keep it?

If such a degree of success even exists, it’s certainly not available to a woman like Misty. Played to wearily ferocious perfection by “Slow Horses” powerhouse Rosalind Eleazar in what should be a star-making performance (but you never know in this town!), the almost 40-year-old Misty has developed a full script of excuses for the downward spiral she’s been on since winning an Emmy for a TV show called “Red Eye” in 2008.

“Too Black to be with Leo, not Black enough to be with Damson, not a nepo baby or a Brit.” She lays it out with a battle-worn intensity that deflects attention from what she’s trying hard not to say; we think “it’s a funny meta-joke that Eleazar is a Brit,” and “is Damson Idris really famous enough to belong in that sentence?,” and not “what has Misty done for the last two decades besides making excuses for herself and getting cozy with some old guy who let her live in his spare apartment?”

We get a partial answer to that question after she bumps into Jordan, the director whose “Cinderella” remake was going to launch Misty into the stratosphere until she got coked up out of control and punched him in the face on set (Rock plays the part himself, wise and resigned in a role that warmly reflects how the onetime firebrand has softened with age). She’s so deeply internalized Hollywood’s treatment of Black women that she can’t even give herself a break. So yeah, it’s true that Misty is a complicated person in a business that’s still painfully simple in its approach to race, age, and second chances, but it’s also true that her inestimable talents as an actress are equaled by her gift for self-sabotage. It’s never just one or the other in her adopted city — it’s always both right on top of each other.

item.title: Everytime, 2026 - ★★★★½
item.description:
I don’t believe in an afterlife, but that’s OK because the people I love most are never going to die. Not to me. At least, not in the way they used to before our species began to migrate online, to store our memories in the cloud, and to digitally encode the raw data of our existence onto everything we touch.

My father was born in 1939, the same year that Iowa State College scientists John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built the prototype for the first binary-based computer; in the months after he died 75 years later, I often felt the reflex to reach down and call him from the iPhone that fit inside my pocket. To ask if he’d seen the Rangers game, or to tell him that I’d gotten engaged. I knew that he was gone, of course, but the piece of consumer technology I’d used to connect with him when he was alive had created a separate neural pathway between my brain and his being — a crude one-way network that didn’t begin to break down until much later in my grieving process.

A decade later, those pathways have grown exponentially more complicated and convincing. The emergence of AI has led to a variety of ghoulish attempts at deathlessness and resurrection (from bots that feed on your grandma’s Facebook data to the ChatGPT Theodore Roosevelt who Trump was “honored to be with today” at the former’s Presidential Library), but such products and publicity stunts miss the fact that everyone is already being (temporarily) immortalized on a server farm somewhere, the traces of our existence shed into the digital ether like a Pollock-like splotch of invisible ink.

Charlie Kirk’s face is Twitter’s most ubiquitous meme. My long-deceased college friend you’ve never heard of sends me hacked emails full of links to “old pictures they found of us together.” The cancer-stricken hedgehog I fostered for a few months in 2016 still cycles onto my home screen at random sometimes, and he’s now been buried behind a house in suburban New Jersey for longer than he was ever alive. People have always looked for errant glimmers of the dead in the world around them, but now the past runs parallel to — imprints upon, and circles around — the present to a degree that can severely confuse the relationship between the two.

Sandra Wollner doesn’t believe in an afterlife either, but she’s certainly attuned to the mysteries of this one. Picking up where the equally spectral likes of “Personal Shopper” and “Aftersun” left up, the Austrian writer/director’s mystical and magnificently beguiling “Everytime” takes a rather ambivalent stance towards what happens when people die these days, or at least — per its curious title — towards how we mourn them from inside the flat circle of a temporal overlap where yesterday and tomorrow are folded into the pockets of an ever-expanding now.

There are no clear answers to be found in this astonishing third feature, which shares a number of thematic similarities with Wollner’s “The Trouble with Being Born,” but retains one crucial difference (that film, about a man who has an implied sexual relationship with a child-sized android coded with the memories of his missing 10-year-old daughter, unsurprisingly had trouble securing American distribution). Indeed, the grounded portraiture of the movie’s first 70 minutes eventually gives way to a final act so cosmic and surreal that it becomes all but impossible to pinpoint the precise location of Wollner’s characters in space-time; to say for certain whether “Everytime” has glitched into another dimension, or if it has invited another dimension to glitch into our own. Initially timeless in its nuanced and deeply recognizable depiction of loss, and then even more so as it gets devoured by the meta-modern flourishes that have fringed its story from the start, this is perhaps the most forward-thinking film I’ve ever seen about the changing face of grief.

His marriage to literary executive Sofia (a sorely under-written role played by Bardem’s real-life wife Penélope Cruz) has withered in the growing shadow of his celebrity profile. He can barely communicate with his phone-addicted teenage daughter, he doesn’t have any time to play with the younger one who’s nearing the end of her cutest years, and his every waking thought is consumed by the window-sized hole that his next-door neighbor (Stephen Graham) has just hammered into the wall that separates their properties. That’s when Miguel receives a heavily NDA-ed offer to design a doomsday bunker for a famous tech billionaire who’s even richer and more detached from the rest of humanity than he is (Paul Dano, whose deeply unnerving one-scene performance cuts to the core of Silicon Valley nihilism with a sharpness that makes him so much scarier than any of the other Zuckerberg-coded villains who’ve seeped into movies over the last 15 years).

If the success they’ve achieved has brought them to this, of what use was the success?

After “The Father” (extraordinary) and “The Son” (not), Zellner has returned with a characteristically bleak vision of the holy ghost; in this case, the invisible specter of fear that causes so many of the modern world’s richest and/or most accomplished people to isolate themselves from the rest of humanity in response to their good fortune. Similar to both of the writer-director’s previous films, the hermetically sealed “Bunker” hinges upon how the architecture of psychology is reflected by the psychology of architecture — it’s fascinated by how people express themselves through the spaces they inhabit and vice-versa. The “organic minimalism” of the mansion that Miguel has designed for his family reveals his utopian desire for light and transparency, but the house’s austere interior, hostile swatches of color, and walled-off garden betray the same closed-off severity that has started to distance Miguel from even his wife and kids.

What do you get for the man who has everything? The impossible peace of mind that no one is going to take it away from him. In a movie that doesn’t leave enough oxygen for laughter, the fact that Miguel is confused why Dano’s character wants to build himself a giant hole in the ground — secure enough to inure him against social collapse, ecological devastation, and even his own bodyguards — is maybe the closest thing we get to a decent joke.

item.title: Look Back, 2026 - ★★★½
item.description:
The magic trick of Kiyotaka Oshiyama’s 53-minute anime film “Look Back” is how its brevity gives visceral dimension to the defining tension of its story: That between the time it takes to create something (in this case, a portfolio of one-shots), and the time it takes to consume it. By contrast, the magic trick of Hirokazu Kore-eda’s 100-minute live-action “Look Back” is that it somehow manages to accomplish the same thing despite running twice as long.

As slavishly faithful to Oshiyama’s anime as Oshiyama’s anime was to Tatsuki Fujimoto’s original manga, Kore-eda’s muted but affecting drama retells the bittersweet tale of two very different schoolgirls in western Japan who are bonded together by their shared love of comics. The popular and boisterous Fujino (expressively played through her tweenage years by Furi Nanase) is famous among her classmates for the yonkoma cartoons that she draws for the school newspaper, and carried by the unique self-confidence that comes from discovering your purpose in life at such a young age. Alas, Fujino’s entire worldview is rattled off its axis when she’s in fourth grade — when a severely anxious local shut-in named Kyomoto begins to submit yonkoma of her own as a tentative way of engaging with the world beyond her bedroom. The recluse’s work naturally lacks the finger-on-the-pulse wit of Fujino’s strips, but it compensates for that with the careful attention of its linework and background detail. A heated rivalry is born.

That rivalry eventually blossoms into a beautiful collaboration, as Fujino is tasked with delivering Kyomoto’s diploma to the shut-in’s seemingly abandoned house at the end of sixth grade (no version of this story makes any mention of her parents’ whereabouts, but the director of “Nobody Knows” can’t help but charge this brief glimpse of Kyomoto’s barren home life with a tacit sense of tragedy), and, in what feels like a predestined twist of fate, inadvertently draws the recluse out of her room. By that point, Fujino’s natural resentment towards Kyomoto’s ability — and her obsessive failure to outdo it — has caused her to question her purpose, but it turns out that Kyomoto is Fujino’s biggest fan, and so Fujino agrees to an ego–saving creative partnership. Half a lifetime down the road, she will be haunted by that decision as if it just happened yesterday. But first: happiness.
